title: The Slave Who Invented Smallpox Inoculation
location: Boston, Massachusetts (knowledge originating from West Africa)
event_summary: An enslaved West African man named Onesimus told his owner, the Puritan minister Cotton Mather, about a practice common in his homeland: deliberately introducing material from a smallpox pustule into a small wound to produce mild illness and lifelong immunity. Mather, initially skeptical, investigated further and found the technique was widespread across West Africa and the Ottoman world. When a devastating smallpox epidemic struck Boston in 1721, Mather persuaded physician Zabdiel Boylston to perform the procedure on 242 people, of whom only six died — a mortality rate of about 2%, compared to nearly 15% among the naturally infected.
why_forgotten: Onesimus's contribution was deliberately minimized because crediting an enslaved African with advanced medical knowledge contradicted the racial ideologies that justified slavery. Mather himself took most of the credit in his published letters to the Royal Society. Over time, the story of inoculation became attached to Edward Jenner's later cowpox vaccine of 1796, further erasing the African origins of the core concept.
why_it_matters: Onesimus's knowledge introduced the principle of deliberate immunization to Western medicine decades before Jenner, laying the intellectual groundwork for vaccination itself — the single most life-saving medical intervention in human history. The 1721 Boston experiment was one of the first controlled public health trials ever conducted, establishing statistical evidence as a basis for medical policy. Every modern vaccine program, from polio to COVID-19, descends conceptually from the practice an enslaved man carried across the Atlantic in his memory.
